mcqs.question: You pull an updated version of an image where only the last instruction changed. Why is the pull usually fast?
options: Docker always re-downloads the entire image regardless of what changed
Fast pulls only happen for images under 100MB
The manifest itself contains all the file contents, so no layers need downloading
Docker only fetches the layers it doesn't already have locally, reusing the rest
mcqs.explanation: A pull fetches the manifest, then compares layer hashes against what's cached locally, downloading only the layers that are new or changed. If only the last instruction changed, only its layer (and anything after it) needs to be fetched.

mcqs.question: A Dockerfile runs `COPY . .` (copying all source code) before `RUN npm install`. What's the main downside of this instruction order?
options: Any source code change invalidates the cache for COPY, which then forces npm install to rerun even if dependencies didn't change
There is no downside — order never affects build behavior
This order makes the final image significantly larger
Docker will refuse to build a Dockerfile in this order
mcqs.explanation: Once a layer's cache misses, every subsequent layer must rebuild too. Copying source before installing dependencies means every code change reruns the expensive install step — reversing the order (install deps first, copy code last) avoids this.

mcqs.question: Your deployment pipeline needs a guarantee that it's running the exact same image build that passed testing, with no possibility of it silently changing. What should it reference?
options: A mutable version tag like `:1.4` that could be repointed
mcqs.explanation: A digest is a content hash — it can only refer to one exact set of bytes and never changes meaning. Tags, including semantic version tags, are mutable labels that can technically be repointed to a different image later.
